prompt: Why does the shop put its approval on the environment shop-production rather than in the pipeline's YAML?
hint: Who can delete a line of YAML?

choices.text: Approvals in YAML are not supported by Azure Pipelines
choices.why: The point is not support; it is who controls the protection.

choices.text: So every pipeline that targets it waits
choices.why: Right. A check on the environment cannot be removed by editing one pipeline.

choices.text: Environment approvals are cheaper per parallel job
choices.why: Checks are not billed per job; the reason is control.

choices.text: Because the environment is where the agents run
choices.why: Agents come from a pool; the environment is the target.

prompt: A deployment reaches shop-production on a Tuesday at 10:00. The approval was granted, but an Azure Monitor alert fired on rg-shop five minutes ago. What happens?

choices.text: It starts, because a person approved it
choices.why: An approval is one of the checks; the job waits for every one.

choices.text: It waits until the alerts gate passes
choices.why: Right. Every check has to pass, and the gate is re-evaluated until it passes or times out.

choices.text: It starts in the staging slot and stops before the swap
choices.why: Checks run before the job starts; nothing is deployed while one is failing.

choices.text: It is cancelled and has to be queued again tomorrow
choices.why: The gate waits and re-evaluates; it fails only at its time-out.

prompt: What is the useful approval setting the lesson recommends, and why?
hint: Whose eyes does an approval add?

choices.text: Allowing any project member, so deployments are never blocked
choices.why: Then the author can approve, and the approval adds no second person.

choices.text: An approval that never times out
choices.why: A waiting approval should fail eventually; a deployment nobody approved should not linger.

choices.text: Refusing the person who queued the run
choices.why: Right. Otherwise an approval is a delay rather than a second pair of eyes.

choices.text: Requiring three approvers on every environment
choices.why: The count is a choice per environment; what matters most is who is excluded.

prompt: Match each check on shop-production to what it protects against.

pairs.right: A change nobody but its author looked at
A deployment when nobody is around to watch
Deploying into an incident already under way
Two runs racing into the same slot

right_distractors: A build that fails its unit tests

prompt: What does App Service do before it switches routing in a swap?
hint: Where does the cold start happen?

choices.text: Starts staging's processes with production's settings and waits until they answer
choices.why: Right. The warm-up happens before any customer request reaches the new version.

choices.text: Copies the production database into the staging slot
choices.why: A swap never touches data.

choices.text: Rebuilds the image from the commit
choices.why: Nothing is rebuilt; the slot already runs the new version.

choices.text: Asks the pipeline's approvers again
choices.why: Approvals belong to the pipeline's environment, before the deployment; the swap does not consult them.

prompt: After a swap, production starts writing orders into the staging database. What was missing?
hint: Which settings travel with the code?

choices.text: Swap with preview
choices.why: Preview lets you test before completing; it would have shown the problem, not prevented it.

choices.text: Marking DB_CONNECTION as slot-specific
choices.why: Right. A sticky setting stays with its slot; an ordinary one travels with the code.

choices.text: A health check path on the staging slot
choices.why: Health checks decide when processes are ready, not which database they use.

choices.text: Auto swap, which would have swapped both slots at once
choices.why: Auto swap is the same swap with nobody looking; it carries settings the same way.

prompt: Why does the shop not turn on auto swap for production?

choices.text: Auto swap skips the warm-up
choices.why: It warms up like any swap.

choices.text: Auto swap works only in the Free tier
choices.why: It is a feature of plans that have slots.

choices.text: It also swaps the sticky settings
choices.why: Sticky settings stay with their slot in every swap.

choices.text: Nobody looks before it swaps
choices.why: Right. Every deployment to staging goes straight to production.

prompt: Production misbehaves ten minutes after a swap. What is the fastest way back to the previous version?
hint: Where is the previous version now?

choices.text: Re-run the previous pipeline run to rebuild and redeploy it
choices.why: That works, and takes as long as a build and deployment.

choices.text: Swap again
choices.why: Right. Staging holds the previous version, already warm.

choices.text: Restore the app from last night's backup
choices.why: A backup restores more than the code and takes longer than a swap.

choices.text: Wait for the diagnosis, then deploy a fix forward
choices.why: The shop's rule is to swap back first and investigate second.

prompt: Release 42 renamed `delivery_slot` to `delivery_window` in one migration. Production fails, and the team swaps back to 41. What happens?
hint: Did the swap touch the table?

choices.text: 41 runs normally, because the swap restored the old schema
choices.why: A swap exchanges code and configuration, never data.

choices.text: The swap is refused while a migration is pending
choices.why: App Service knows nothing about the database's migrations.

choices.text: 41 queries a column that no longer exists, and fails too
choices.why: Right. That is why changes to shared data are split into expand and contract.

choices.text: Both columns exist, so either version works
choices.why: That would be expand-then-contract; a rename in one step leaves one column.

prompt: Put the expand-and-contract change to the orders table in order.
items: Wait until nobody will swap back to 41
trap: Dropping the old column in the same release as adding the new one is the slip: the swap back then meets a column that is gone.

prompt: A team's App Service plan has no slots in its tier, and they want this lesson's pattern. What is the honest answer?
hint: Does the pattern exist without slots?

choices.text: Use swap with preview, which needs no slot
choices.why: Preview is a kind of swap, and a swap needs a slot.

choices.text: Deploy twice to production, once to warm it up
choices.why: The first deployment already lands on customers.

choices.text: Move to a tier with slots, or deploy in place
choices.why: Right. Slots depend on the plan's tier; checking that first is part of the design.

choices.text: Create a second resource group and swap between them
choices.why: A swap is between slots of one app, not between resource groups.

prompt: The shop's rule watches `POST /checkout` for a fixed window after each swap before it calls the release good. How many minutes is that window?
hint: It is in the rollback section.

prompt: Which of these can a swap back to the previous version undo? Choose all that apply.
hint: Code and configuration, yes; data, no.

choices.text: A bug in the new code
choices.why: Yes. The previous code is what runs after the swap.

choices.text: A wrong app setting that travelled with the new version
choices.why: Yes. Ordinary settings travel with the code, both ways.

choices.text: Rows the new version wrote in a new format
choices.why: No. Data stays as the new version left it.

choices.text: A column the new version's migration dropped
choices.why: No. That is exactly what expand and contract exists for.
